content: The swelling and mucus production in the airways that occur during an acute asthma attack are most effectively managed with anti-inflammatory medications, such as corticosteroids. These can be administered through inhalation, orally, intravenously, or via intramuscular injection. However, there is ongoing debate regarding the use of systemic corticosteroids in the early management of acute asthma for patients presenting to the emergency department (ED). The objective of this study was to evaluate the benefits of administering systemic corticosteroids to patients with acute asthma within one hour of their arrival at the ED. To achieve this, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were identified through the Cochrane Airways Group Asthma Register. Additionally, primary authors and experts in the field were contacted to identify eligible studies, and bibliographies of included studies and relevant reviews were examined. Only RCTs or quasi-randomized trials were considered for inclusion. Studies were eligible if they involved patients presenting to the ED with acute asthma who were treated with systemic corticosteroids (either intravenous, intramuscular, or oral) versus a placebo within one hour of arrival. The studies also needed to report either hospital admission rates or pulmonary function outcomes. Data collection, trial selection, and quality assessment were conducted independently by two reviewers and verified with the corresponding authors. The analysis included 12 studies involving a total of 863 patients, with 435 receiving corticosteroids and 428 receiving a placebo. The early administration of systemic corticosteroids in the ED significantly reduced hospital admission rates. Specifically, the pooled odds ratio (OR) for admission was 0.40 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.21 to 0.78), which translates to a number needed to treat (NNT) of 8 (95% CI: 5 to 21). The benefit was more pronounced in patients who had not received systemic corticosteroids prior to arriving at the ED (OR: 0.37, 95% CI: 0.19 to 0.70) and in those with more severe asthma (OR: 0.35, 95% CI: 0.21 to 0.59). In children, oral corticosteroid therapy was particularly effective, with an OR of 0.24 (95% CI: 0.11 to 0.53). However, no trials involving adults used the oral route for corticosteroid administration. Importantly, the side effects associated with corticosteroid treatment were not significantly different from those observed with placebo. An updated search conducted in September 2002 did not identify any additional trials. In conclusion, the administration of systemic corticosteroids within one hour of presentation to the ED significantly reduces the likelihood of hospital admission for patients experiencing acute asthma. The benefits are most notable in patients with more severe asthma and those who were not already receiving corticosteroid therapy. Children, in particular, appear to respond well to oral corticosteroids.
